This is a good article that adequately starts to deal with the frequent misuse of the 77 cent to the dollar figure.

That 60% of the disparity which can be explained by correcting for years of experience, industry and hours worked cuts the disparity to 90.5 cents to the dollar (23c the total gap from 77c, 60% off that 23c is 13.8c explained by those corrections). This is the figure people should be using for the 'same work same pay' statistic.

I'm not sure I agree with the author that the 40% of the 77 cent disparity is particularly useful. It accounts for self selection based on personal interest and perhaps a degree of societal pressure. However all too often people attribute this to women being forced into these choices, as opposed to choosing them given today's societal context. The interpretation of the 40% is highly subjective.

My opinion, they should be considered separately. The 90.5c is the real minimum disparity from which discussions start but more may exist based on personal choice and societal pressure. I don't necessarily buy into the idea that the 40% is entirely due to sexism or wholly negligible. Note also that using the weekly data figure instead (82.1c to the dollar without correction), this wage gap excluding the 60% objective demographic correction: falls to 6.4 cents, listing women earning 93.6cents to the dollar. My opinion is that weekly earnings are more accurate as they are less prone to further demographic shocks (e.g. taking maternity leave will drop an annual income significantly, but weekly does not take as severe a hit).

Additionally, I'm not sure I find the finding regarding hour disparities shocking. If you consider the additional hours men work as overtime, it should not come as a surprise that it is paid out at a premium higher than their other hours. Hours worked are not equally compensated, each additional hour comes at a premium. Whether officially compensated as overtime or not.
